analogy.p: Judging a product by one stage is like judging a takeaway coffee only by the price on the till. The real cost includes growing and roasting the beans, shipping them, making the cup and lid, the electricity for the machine, and the bin the cup ends up in. An LCA adds up all of those steps. The part about value judgements is like arguing about whether the waste from the cup matters more than the shipping of the beans: a calculator cannot settle that. The analogy breaks down because coffee costs are all in pounds, whereas environmental impacts are measured in different units that cannot be added together simply.
analogy.t: The full price of a takeaway coffee

bullets: **Definition to learn:** an LCA assesses the environmental impact of a product over its whole life, in each of four stages.
The four stages are: **extracting and processing raw materials**, **manufacturing and packaging**, **use and operation during its lifetime**, and **disposal at the end of its life**.
**Transport and distribution** are included at every stage, not just once.
The aim is to compare products or processes fairly, for example plastic bags against paper bags.
LCAs help companies cut energy and waste, and help governments set rules on packaging and recycling.
LCA is part of **sustainable development**: meeting the needs of people today without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
The environmental impact is judged by what is used up (resources, energy, water) and what is given out (wastes, emissions, pollutants).
core.h: What a life cycle assessment is and why it is carried out
core.p: A **life cycle assessment (LCA)** is a method used to assess the **environmental impact** of a product at every stage of its life, from the moment the raw materials are taken from the Earth until the product is thrown away or recycled. It is carried out so that people can compare products and decide which one does less harm to the environment. LCAs are used by manufacturers, governments and campaign groups, and examiners like to ask you to use LCA data to make or judge a decision. The key idea is that the damage a product does is not only caused when you use it, so you have to look at the **whole life** of the product.

bullets: **Stage 1 – raw materials:** getting materials out of the ground or growing them, then processing them (for example refining crude oil, or turning wood into pulp).
**Stage 2 – manufacture and packaging:** turning materials into the product and packing it ready for sale.
**Stage 3 – use and operation:** the energy, water and other resources used while the product is in service, plus how long it lasts and whether it can be reused.
**Stage 4 – disposal:** what happens when it is finished with: landfill, burning, recycling or reuse.
**Transport and distribution** by lorry, ship, train or plane use fuel and give out carbon dioxide at every stage.
Memory trick: **R-M-U-D** (Raw materials, Making, Use, Disposal) with **T** for transport running underneath.
core.h: The four stages at a glance
core.p: Every LCA is organised into the same four stages, which makes comparisons fair. For each stage you ask the same questions: how much **energy** is used, how much **water** is used, which **raw materials** are used up, and what **wastes** and pollution are produced. You then add up the answers across all four stages (with transport included) to get the overall picture. A product that looks good at one stage can look bad when the whole life is counted, and that is the main point of doing an LCA.

bullets: Plastic carrier bags are made from **crude oil**, a finite resource that must be extracted, transported and refined.
Paper bags are made from **trees**, which are renewable if forests are replanted, but growing and pulping wood uses land, water and energy.
Farming crops for materials uses water, fertiliser and land, and may remove habitats.
Extracting metals from ores uses a lot of energy and can produce waste rock and polluting gases such as sulfur dioxide.
Renewable raw materials are not automatically better: you still have to count the energy and water used to process them.
Recycled raw materials usually need less energy than new ones, which is why recycling is linked to LCA.
In an exam, name the **specific** raw material and say whether it is renewable or finite.
core.h: Stage 1: extracting and processing raw materials
core.p: The first stage covers everything needed to get hold of the materials that the product is made from. Quarrying and mining destroy habitats, create dust, noise and waste rock, and use large amounts of energy. Many raw materials are **finite resources**, for example crude oil, metal ores and sand, so using them up makes them unavailable for the future. Processing them, such as fractional distillation of crude oil or extracting a metal from its ore, is often energy-hungry and much of that energy comes from burning **fossil fuels**, which releases carbon dioxide.

bullets: Typical measurements are the **energy used** (in joules or megajoules) and the **water used** (in dm3) per item made.
Products that are heavier or bulkier need more material and more fuel to transport.
Making paper bags needs more energy and water than making plastic bags of the same carrying capacity (in the usual textbook comparison).
Waste produced in manufacturing can be reused or recycled in the factory to reduce its impact.
Packaging is part of the product's life cycle: it uses resources, adds mass for transport and must be disposed of.
Manufacturing on an industrial scale usually involves chemical reactions and heating, so energy efficiency matters.
Quote **numbers** from the data (for example 'paper uses 1.5 MJ compared with 0.6 MJ') whenever you are given a table.
core.p: In the second stage the processed materials are made into the finished product and packed. Factories use electricity and heat, which are normally generated by burning fossil fuels, so this stage often produces a large share of the total carbon dioxide. Manufacturing also uses water for cooling and cleaning and produces waste, such as offcuts and polluted water. Packaging has its own life cycle, since it needs raw materials, energy and disposal, which is why excess packaging is criticised.

bullets: For appliances, this stage includes **electricity or fuel used** and water used during operation.
For bags, it includes strength, durability and how often they are **reused** before being thrown away.
Paper bags tear when wet and so are often used only once; plastic bags are often reused several times.
To compare fairly, divide the total impact by the number of uses to get the impact **per use**.
A product with a high manufacturing impact can still be the better choice if it lasts long enough.
Maintenance, repairs and cleaning also count towards this stage.
Longer lasting products also reduce the demand for new raw materials.
core.h: Stage 3: use and operation during the product's lifetime
core.p: The third stage looks at what happens while the product is in service. For some products this is the biggest impact: a car or a washing machine uses energy and water for years, while a carrier bag uses none, so for a bag the key question is **how many times it can be reused**. A product that lasts longer or is used many times spreads its manufacturing impact over more uses, so the impact **per use** is lower. This is why a heavy-duty bag reused many times can beat a single-use bag.

bullets: **Plastics** made from poly(ethene) are not biodegradable, so they last a very long time in landfill and can harm wildlife if littered.
**Paper** is biodegradable, so it rots, although rotting in landfill can release methane, a greenhouse gas.
Burning waste can recover energy but releases carbon dioxide and may release other pollutants.
Both plastic and paper bags can be recycled, but the recycling itself needs energy and transport.
Reuse (using the item again as it is) usually has a lower impact than recycling because nothing needs to be melted or remade.
Waste sent to landfill uses up land and may leak pollutants into soil and water.
State whether the material is **biodegradable** and what the likely disposal route is.
core.h: Stage 4: disposal at the end of life
core.p: The final stage covers what happens when the product has no further use. The options are **landfill**, **burning (incineration)**, **reuse** and **recycling**, and each has an environmental cost. Landfill takes up land and some materials do not decompose, while burning gives out carbon dioxide and possibly toxic gases. Recycling and reuse reduce the demand for new raw materials, but collecting, sorting and reprocessing also need energy. Disposal is also where **biodegradability** matters, because materials that microorganisms can break down cause less long-term waste.

bullets: Fuel for lorries, ships, trains and planes is mostly made from crude oil, a finite resource.
Transport produces **carbon dioxide**, and diesel engines can also produce particulates and oxides of nitrogen.
Local sourcing of materials reduces the distance travelled and so the fuel used.
Heavier products require more fuel to move the same distance.
Moving raw materials, moving part-finished parts to a factory and moving finished goods to shops are all counted.
Collecting waste and recycling materials also involves transport.
Do not forget transport in your answers: it is a quick extra mark in a '4 stages' question.
core.h: Transport and distribution at every stage
core.p: Materials and products are carried between each of the stages and then to shops and homes. Transport uses fuel, usually from crude oil, and releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants, so it is included at every stage rather than being treated as a separate fifth stage. A heavier product or a longer journey means more fuel burned, so **mass** and **distance** both matter. This is the reason why the mass of a paper bag compared with a plastic bag is a relevant point in the comparison.

bullets: **Quantifiable:** the amount of water used, the mass and type of resources used, energy used, and some wastes (for example mass of waste produced).
**Not easy to quantify:** the harm done by pollutants, damage to habitats, visual pollution and risks to health.
Quantities are measured in sensible units: MJ for energy, dm3 for water, g or kg for mass of materials and waste.
Different pollutants have different effects, so you cannot simply add them up.
Someone has to decide how important each effect is: that is a **value judgement**.
Two people with the same data can reach different conclusions about which product is 'greener'.
core.h: What can be measured and what cannot
core.p: Some parts of an LCA can be given **numerical values** easily. The **use of water**, **resources**, **energy sources** and the **production of some wastes** can be quantified, for example 'the process uses 3 dm3 of water' or 'it gives out 40 g of carbon dioxide'. Other things are much harder to measure. The **effect of pollutants** on the environment, such as harm to wildlife, loss of habitat or damage to people's health, is difficult to turn into a single number. For this reason an LCA always combines numbers with opinions.

bullets: Objective means based only on measurable facts; **value judgements are subjective**.
Deciding how to **score** the harm from one pollutant against another needs a judgement.
The choice of which stages and impacts to include is also a judgement.
The same LCA data may be used to argue for different products depending on which impact is considered most important.
A fair LCA should be open about the data and the judgements made, so other people can check them.
Model phrase: 'Value judgements are needed because pollutant effects cannot be given exact numerical values.'
core.h: Value judgements: why an LCA is not purely objective
core.p: A **value judgement** is a decision about how important something is, and it depends on opinions rather than on measurement alone. **Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects is less straightforward and requires value judgements**, so a life cycle assessment is not a purely objective process. For example, is it worse to use a lot of water or to produce a lot of carbon dioxide? Different people, companies and countries give different answers. If the people who carry out the LCA weigh the effects in a way that suits their product, the result can be biased.

bullets: **Selective / abbreviated LCA:** a shortened assessment that leaves out stages or impacts.
Misuse: only presenting the data that makes the company's own product look better than rivals.
Example: an advert for a bottle that only mentions the low energy used in use, but not the energy used to make it.
A claim is more trustworthy if it is checked by an independent organisation.
Look for missing information: which stages, which pollutants, what the comparison is with.
Model phrase: 'The advert may be biased because it only considers one stage of the life cycle.'
Never say 'LCAs are useless': say they are useful but can be misused if selective.
core.h: Selective and abbreviated LCAs, and how they can be misused
core.p: A full LCA is expensive and slow, so companies sometimes carry out a **selective** or **abbreviated LCA**, which only looks at some stages or some impacts. These shortened versions can be useful for quick comparisons, but they can also be **misused**, especially to support claims in **advertising**. A company could, for example, count only the stage where its product performs well and ignore the stages where it performs badly, and then claim that its product is 'green'. When you read an advertisement, always ask which stages were left out and who carried out the assessment.

bullets: Raw materials: plastic = crude oil (finite, non-renewable); paper = wood from trees (renewable if replanted).
Manufacture: paper often uses **more energy and more water** than plastic for each bag.
Mass: paper bags are heavier, so transport uses more fuel.
Use: plastic bags are generally more durable and can be reused; paper bags tear and are often used once.
Disposal: plastic is **not biodegradable** and persists in landfill; paper is biodegradable and can be recycled.
Overall conclusion: neither bag is automatically best; a plastic bag that is reused many times can have a lower impact **per use** than a paper bag used once.
Always back your conclusion with **numbers from the data** and say what you are weighing up.
core.h: Comparative LCA: plastic and paper shopping bags
core.p: The specification asks you to **carry out simple comparative LCAs for shopping bags made from plastic and paper**, so you must be able to go through the four stages for each bag and reach a judgement. At stage 1 plastic comes from finite crude oil while paper comes from renewable trees. At stage 2 the typical comparison is that paper bags need more energy and water to make and are heavier to transport. At stage 3 plastic bags are stronger and reused more often, whereas paper bags tear when wet. At stage 4 paper rots and plastic does not, but both can be recycled. Overall, the 'best' bag depends on the data given and on how many times each bag is reused.

bullets: Impact per use = total impact of one item ÷ number of times it is used.
Total energy = energy for stage 1 + stage 2 + stage 3 + stage 4 (plus transport if given separately).
Percentage of total = (value for one stage ÷ total) × 100.
Compare using a ratio: 'paper uses 7.5 times as much energy per use' is stronger than 'paper uses more'.
Keep the units: MJ, kJ, dm3, g, kg. Do not mix grams and kilograms.
Give answers to a sensible number of significant figures (usually 2 or 3).
If asked for a conclusion, mention **limitations**: values might be estimates and some impacts are not included.
core.h: Working with LCA data: per-use calculations and percentages
core.p: Many exam questions give a table of data and expect you to do a short calculation before you write a conclusion. The most useful tools are **impact per use** (total impact divided by the number of uses), **total impact over all stages** (add the stages together) and **percentage contribution** of one stage (stage divided by total, multiplied by 100). Always show the working, give the unit, and then link the result to a decision. Check that you are comparing like with like, for example the same unit and the same number of bags.

bullets: Link to **organic chemistry:** poly(ethene) is made from ethene, which comes from cracking fractions of crude oil.
Link to **atmosphere:** burning fossil fuels at any stage releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas.
Link to **recycling:** recycling affects stage 1 (less new raw material) and stage 4 (less waste).
Link to **potable water and sustainability:** using less water and energy is more sustainable.
Higher-tier style question: **evaluate** an LCA claim by pointing out missing stages and value judgements.
An LCA cannot tell you what to do: it informs a decision, which also involves cost and values.
core.h: Using LCAs to make decisions and link to other topics
core.p: LCAs are only one piece of evidence in a decision. Governments might use them to decide whether to charge for plastic bags, companies to redesign packaging, and shoppers to decide what to buy. Cost, convenience, safety and public opinion also matter. An LCA also connects to many other parts of the specification: **polymers** (what plastic is made from), **crude oil and fractional distillation**, **recycling and reusing** materials, **fossil fuels and carbon dioxide emissions** (climate change), and **sustainable development**. Seeing these links helps you pick relevant points in longer written answers.

bullets: '**Give** the four stages' – name them exactly: raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, disposal.
'**Explain why** LCAs are not objective' – pollutant effects need value judgements.
'**Evaluate**' – give advantages and disadvantages of each option and a justified conclusion.
'**Compare**' – use words like 'whereas' and 'however', and refer to both products each time.
Use numbers from the table with units.
Mention transport and note that some data may be missing or estimated.
Avoid vague words such as 'bad for the environment': say what kind of damage.
core.p: LCA questions usually appear as 2 to 6 mark questions, often on Paper 2, with data in a table. To get full marks, you need to use the correct **stage names**, quote **data**, and give a reasoned conclusion. In a 6-mark question the mark scheme is level based: you need a balanced answer that deals with both products across several stages, uses numbers, notes limitations, and finishes with a justified conclusion. Practise writing a short sentence for each stage and then a final 'overall' sentence.

exam: 'Give the stages of an LCA' (up to 4 marks, 1 each): extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation; disposal. Add 'transport at each stage' if the question allows.
'Explain why an LCA is not purely objective' (2 marks): the effects of pollutants cannot be given exact numerical values (1) so value judgements are needed (1).
'Explain how an LCA could be misused' (2 marks): a selective or abbreviated LCA (1) used to support claims in advertising by ignoring stages that make the product look bad (1).
For a table of data, **always quote values with units** and compare using a ratio or difference.

6-mark 'evaluate' answers: use headings in your head (raw materials, making, use, disposal), compare both products at each stage, include a calculation, state a limitation and end with a justified conclusion.
Use the command word: **describe** = what happens; **explain** = because; **evaluate** = weigh up and conclude; **compare** = similarities and differences of both.
Avoid vague terms like 'worse for the environment': say 'uses more energy' or 'does not biodegrade'.
Model sentences: 'The paper bag uses more energy to make (1.5 MJ compared with 0.6 MJ) but ...'; 'However, the plastic bag is made from crude oil, a finite resource.'
Calculations: show the working line (for example 0.6 ÷ 3 = 0.2 MJ per use) and finish with the unit.
If a question says 'use the information', refer directly to the data given rather than your own memory.
Check whether the question wants one product or a **comparison**; for a comparison, write about both in each sentence.

mistakes.r: An LCA covers the whole life: raw materials, manufacture and packaging, use, and disposal, with transport at every stage.
mistakes.w: An LCA only looks at the pollution made while the product is being used.

mistakes.r: Paper bags often use more energy and water to make, are heavier to transport and are reused less; the answer must use the data.
mistakes.w: Paper bags are always better because they come from trees and rot.

mistakes.r: A plastic bag reused many times can have a lower impact per use; state both the disadvantage (finite oil, not biodegradable) and the advantage.
mistakes.w: Plastic bags are always worse because they are made from oil.

mistakes.r: Only some inputs, such as water, energy and some wastes, can be quantified; pollutant effects need value judgements, so an LCA is not purely objective.
mistakes.w: LCAs give exact, accurate numbers for everything.

mistakes.r: Transport and distribution are included at each of the four stages.
Biodegradable means it can be broken down by microorganisms; it can still cause problems, for example releasing methane in landfill.
mistakes.w: Biodegradable means that it is harmless.

mistakes.r: Selective or abbreviated LCAs can be misused for advertising; check which stages and impacts were considered.
mistakes.w: An advert says its product is 'green', so it must be.

mistakes.r: Growing and processing renewable materials still uses energy, water and land.
mistakes.w: Renewable raw materials have no environmental impact.

summary: Describe the four stages of a life cycle assessment (raw materials, manufacture and packaging, use, disposal, with transport at every stage), explain why LCA is not purely objective, and carry out simple comparative LCAs such as plastic versus paper shopping bags. It matters because LCA data questions need you to quote numbers, compare products and justify a conclusion.

terms.d: A method of assessing the environmental impact of a product at each stage of its life: extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use and operation, and disposal, including transport and distribution at each stage.
A natural material taken from the Earth or grown, which is used to make a product.
A resource that is used up faster than it can be replaced, for example crude oil and metal ores.
A resource that can be replaced as fast as it is used, for example trees if replanted.
Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
To give a numerical value to something, for example the mass of waste or the volume of water used.
A decision about how important or harmful something is, based on opinion rather than purely measurable data.
Based on measurable facts and not influenced by personal opinion.
A shortened life cycle assessment that considers only some stages or impacts, and can be misused, for example in advertising.
A substance that is harmful to the environment or to living organisms.
Able to be broken down by microorganisms into simpler substances.
A site where waste is buried; it takes up land and can leak pollutants.
Material used to wrap or protect a product; it also has its own life cycle.
A fuel formed from the remains of living things over millions of years, for example crude oil, coal and natural gas.
Moving materials, parts and finished goods between stages and to consumers, which uses fuel and produces emissions.
An LCA that compares two or more products, such as plastic and paper bags, using the same stages and measures.
Using an item again, either for the same purpose or a new one, without reprocessing it.

worked.ans: Plastic: 0.2 MJ and 0.33 dm3 per use. Paper: 1.5 MJ and 3.0 dm3 per use. The plastic bag has the lower impact per use (paper uses 7.5 times the energy), but this depends on the plastic bag being reused 3 times.
worked.q: The table shows data for two shopping bags. Plastic bag: energy to make 0.6 MJ, water used 1.0 dm3, reused 3 times. Paper bag: energy to make 1.5 MJ, water used 3.0 dm3, used once. Calculate the energy and water per use for each bag and state which has the lower impact per use. (4 marks)
steps: Energy per use = energy to make ÷ number of uses.
Water per use, plastic: 1.0 ÷ 3 = 0.33 dm3 per use (2 s.f.); paper: 3.0 ÷ 1 = 3.0 dm3 per use.
Compare: 1.5 ÷ 0.2 = 7.5, so the paper bag uses 7.5 times as much energy per use.

worked.ans: 50% of the total energy is used in manufacture and packaging.
worked.q: In an LCA of a product, the energy used at each stage is: raw materials 0.20 MJ, manufacture and packaging 0.35 MJ, use 0.05 MJ, disposal 0.10 MJ. Calculate the percentage of the total energy used in manufacture and packaging. (3 marks)

worked.ans: The advert may rely on a selective (abbreviated) LCA that only considers one stage, such as use, and ignores the energy and water used in making and disposing of the bottle, so the claim could be biased. An LCA is not purely objective because allocating numerical values to the effects of pollutants is not straightforward and needs value judgements.
worked.q: A company advertises that its drinks bottle has 'the lowest carbon footprint'. Explain two reasons why the advert may be misleading and explain why an LCA is not purely objective. (4 marks)
steps: Say the company may have used a selective or abbreviated LCA that only looks at some stages.
Say it may have ignored stages that make the bottle look bad, such as manufacture or disposal.
State that the effects of pollutants cannot be given exact numerical values.
So value judgements are needed, which are opinions and not facts.
